subproblem.title: Graph points are the inverse of the canonical equivalence ℝ^{n+ℓ} ≅ ℝⁿ × ℝ^ℓ
subproblem.statement: For all n, ℓ ∈ ℕ, x ∈ ℝⁿ and y ∈ ℝ^ℓ, the graph point graphPoint x y = toLp 2 (Fin.append (ofLp x) (ofLp y)) (the vector of ℝ^{n+ℓ} whose first n coordinates are x and whose last ℓ coordinates are y) equals E.symm (x, y), where E := EuclideanSpace.finAddEquivProd : ℝ^{n+ℓ} ≃L[ℝ] ℝⁿ × ℝ^ℓ is Mathlib's canonical continuous linear equivalence sending z to the pair (first n coordinates of z, last ℓ coordinates of z).
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ {n ℓ : ℕ} (x : Rn n) (y : Rn ℓ), graphPoint x y = (EuclideanSpace.finAddEquivProd : Amb n ℓ ≃L[ℝ] Rn n × Rn ℓ).symm (x, y)
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: step 1 of the parent proof (G(x, y) := graphPoint x y = toLp 2 (Fin.append (ofLp x) (ofLp y)) is linear in the pair (x, y), hence a continuous linear map ℝⁿ × ℝ^ℓ → ℝ^{n+ℓ}, and G(x, y) determines x by comparing the first n coordinates, Fin.append_left); this child makes that precise by identifying G with the inverse of Mathlib's canonical equivalence, by comparing coordinates. Fix n, ℓ ∈ ℕ, x ∈ ℝⁿ, y ∈ ℝ^ℓ, let E := EuclideanSpace.finAddEquivProd : ℝ^{n+ℓ} ≃L[ℝ] ℝⁿ × ℝ^ℓ and w := E.symm (x, y).
1. (Coordinates of E.) By its definition (Mathlib/Analysis/InnerProductSpace/PiL2.lean, section finAddEquivProd), E is the composite of the coordinate reindexing LinearIsometryEquiv.piLpCongrLeft 2 ℝ ℝ finSumFinEquiv.symm : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin (n+ℓ)) → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n ⊕ Fin ℓ), which sends z to the vector b ↦ z (finSumFinEquiv b), with EuclideanSpace.sumEquivProd, which splits a vector indexed by Fin n ⊕ Fin ℓ into its Sum.inl-part and its Sum.inr-part. Since finSumFinEquiv (Sum.inl j) = Fin.castAdd ℓ j and finSumFinEquiv (Sum.inr k) = Fin.natAdd n k (finSumFinEquiv_apply_left/right), for every z ∈ ℝ^{n+ℓ} we get E z = ((z (Fin.castAdd ℓ j))_{j : Fin n}, (z (Fin.natAdd n k))_{k : Fin ℓ}).
2. (Coordinates of w.) Since E is an equivalence, E w = E (E.symm (x, y)) = (x, y). Applying the formula of step 1 to z = w gives (w (Fin.castAdd ℓ j))_{j : Fin n} = x and (w (Fin.natAdd n k))_{k : Fin ℓ} = y, i.e. w (Fin.castAdd ℓ j) = x_j for all j : Fin n and w (Fin.natAdd n k) = y_k for all k : Fin ℓ.
3. (Coordinates of graphPoint x y.) By definition (graphPoint x y)(i) = Fin.append (ofLp x) (ofLp y) i for all i : Fin (n+ℓ), so (graphPoint x y)(Fin.castAdd ℓ j) = x_j (Fin.append_left) and (graphPoint x y)(Fin.natAdd n k) = y_k (Fin.append_right).
4. (Conclusion.) Two vectors of EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin (n+ℓ)) are equal as soon as all their coordinates agree (ext), and every index i : Fin (n+ℓ) is of the form Fin.castAdd ℓ j with j : Fin n or Fin.natAdd n k with k : Fin ℓ (Fin.addCases). By steps 2 and 3 the coordinates of graphPoint x y and of w agree in both cases. Hence graphPoint x y = w = E.symm (x, y). (Lean outline, checked against the pinned Mathlib: ext i; refine Fin.addCases (fun j => ?_) (fun k => ?_) i, then simp [graphPoint] closes each case.)

subproblem.title: Pythagorean identity for graph points
subproblem.statement: For all n, ℓ ∈ ℕ, x ∈ ℝⁿ and y ∈ ℝ^ℓ (Euclidean spaces Rn n = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n), Rn ℓ), the graph point graphPoint x y = toLp 2 (Fin.append (ofLp x) (ofLp y)) ∈ ℝ^{n+ℓ} (first n coordinates x, last ℓ coordinates y) satisfies ‖graphPoint x y‖² = ‖x‖² + ‖y‖² (Euclidean norms).
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ {n ℓ : ℕ} (x : Rn n) (y : Rn ℓ), ‖graphPoint x y‖ ^ 2 = ‖x‖ ^ 2 + ‖y‖ ^ 2
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: step 1 of the parent proof (‖G(x,y)‖² = Σ_{i<n+ℓ} (Fin.append x y)_i² = ‖x‖² + ‖y‖², splitting the sum over Fin (n+ℓ) with Fin.sum_univ_add). Fix n, ℓ ∈ ℕ, x ∈ ℝⁿ, y ∈ ℝ^ℓ and write G := graphPoint x y = toLp 2 (Fin.append (ofLp x) (ofLp y)).
1. For every finite index type ι and every z ∈ EuclideanSpace ℝ ι we have ‖z‖² = Σ_{i ∈ ι} z_i² (EuclideanSpace.real_norm_sq_eq). Applied to G, x and y this gives ‖G‖² = Σ_{i : Fin (n+ℓ)} G_i², ‖x‖² = Σ_{j : Fin n} x_j² and ‖y‖² = Σ_{k : Fin ℓ} y_k².
2. By the definition of graphPoint, G_i = Fin.append (ofLp x) (ofLp y) i for every i : Fin (n+ℓ). Hence for j : Fin n, G_{Fin.castAdd ℓ j} = x_j (Fin.append_left), and for k : Fin ℓ, G_{Fin.natAdd n k} = y_k (Fin.append_right).
3. Every sum over Fin (n+ℓ) splits as Σ_{i : Fin (n+ℓ)} f(i) = Σ_{j : Fin n} f(Fin.castAdd ℓ j) + Σ_{k : Fin ℓ} f(Fin.natAdd n k) (Fin.sum_univ_add). Applying this to f(i) := G_i² and then step 2 gives ‖G‖² = Σ_{j : Fin n} x_j² + Σ_{k : Fin ℓ} y_k².
4. By step 1 the right-hand side of step 3 equals ‖x‖² + ‖y‖². Hence ‖graphPoint x y‖² = ‖x‖² + ‖y‖². (Lean outline, checked against the pinned Mathlib: rw [EuclideanSpace.real_norm_sq_eq, EuclideanSpace.real_norm_sq_eq, EuclideanSpace.real_norm_sq_eq, Fin.sum_univ_add]; simp [graphPoint].)

Split the sum over Fin (n+ℓ) with Fin.sum_univ_add
Recombine the two partial sums into ‖x‖² + ‖y‖²

subproblem.title: Rotated, translated graph map of a C¹ function is an injective C¹ immersion
subproblem.statement: Let n, ℓ ∈ ℕ, q a linear isometry equivalence of ℝ^{n+ℓ}, u : ℝⁿ → ℝ^ℓ, x₀ ∈ ℝ^{n+ℓ} and Ω ⊆ ℝⁿ an open set on which u is C¹ (ContDiffOn ℝ 1 u Ω). Let φ(x) := q(graphPoint x (u x)) + x₀. Then (a) φ is injective on all of ℝⁿ, (b) φ is C¹ on Ω, and (c) for every x ∈ Ω the Fréchet derivative fderiv ℝ φ x is an injective linear map.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ {n ℓ : ℕ} (q : Amb n ℓ ≃ₗᵢ[ℝ] Amb n ℓ) (u : Rn n → Rn ℓ) (x₀ : Amb n ℓ) (Ω : Set (Rn n)), IsOpen Ω → ContDiffOn ℝ 1 u Ω → Function.Injective (fun x => q (graphPoint x (u x)) + x₀) ∧ ContDiffOn ℝ 1 (fun x => q (graphPoint x (u x)) + x₀) Ω ∧ ∀ x ∈ Ω, Function.Injective (fderiv ℝ (fun x => q (graphPoint x (u x)) + x₀) x)
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: steps 1(ii), 4, 5 and 6 of the parent proof, with the parent's chart domain replaced by an arbitrary open set Ω on which u is C¹; in step 6 below the conclusion v = w is drawn from fact 1(ii) of the parent (graph points determine the base point, realised as injectivity of L) instead of the norm inequality 1(i), which gives the same conclusion. Fix the data, write φ(x) := q(graphPoint x (u x)) + x₀, let E := EuclideanSpace.finAddEquivProd : ℝ^{n+ℓ} ≃L[ℝ] ℝⁿ × ℝ^ℓ, let L := E.symm viewed as a continuous linear map ℝⁿ × ℝ^ℓ → ℝ^{n+ℓ}, and let Q := q viewed as a continuous linear map ℝ^{n+ℓ} → ℝ^{n+ℓ}.
1. (Linear form of graph points.) By the sibling lemma rsod_graphPoint_eq_finAddEquivProd_symm, graphPoint a b = L(a, b) for all a ∈ ℝⁿ and b ∈ ℝ^ℓ. Hence φ(x) = (Q ∘ L)(x, u x) + x₀ for every x ∈ ℝⁿ, i.e. φ = (Q ∘ L) ∘ (x ↦ (x, u x)) + x₀.
2. (Graph points determine the base point, parent step 1(ii).) L is the inverse of the equivalence E, hence injective. So if L(a, b) = L(a', b') then (a, b) = (a', b') and in particular a = a' (take first components).
3. (Injectivity, parent step 5.) Suppose φ(x) = φ(x'). Cancelling the common summand x₀ gives q(graphPoint x (u x)) = q(graphPoint x' (u x')); q is injective, so graphPoint x (u x) = graphPoint x' (u x'), i.e. L(x, u x) = L(x', u x') by step 1. By step 2, x = x'. Thus φ is injective on all of ℝⁿ.
4. (C¹ on Ω, parent step 4.) The map x ↦ (x, u x) is C¹ on Ω because the identity is C^∞ and u is C¹ on Ω (ContDiffOn.prodMk). The continuous linear map Q ∘ L is C^∞, so x ↦ (Q ∘ L)(x, u x) is C¹ on Ω (ContinuousLinearMap.contDiff composed with a ContDiffOn map), and adding the constant x₀ preserves this (ContDiffOn.add with contDiffOn_const). By step 1 this function is φ, so φ is C¹ on Ω.
5. (Derivative, parent step 4.) Let x ∈ Ω. Since Ω is open, Ω is a neighbourhood of x, so u is C¹ at x (ContDiffOn.contDiffAt) and in particular differentiable at x (because 1 ≠ 0); write Du(x) := fderiv ℝ u x, so u has Fréchet derivative Du(x) at x. Then x' ↦ (x', u x') has derivative v ↦ (v, Du(x) v) at x (HasFDerivAt.prodMk with hasFDerivAt_id), the continuous linear map Q ∘ L is its own derivative, and adding the constant x₀ does not change the derivative. By the chain rule and step 1, φ has derivative (Q ∘ L) ∘ (id, Du(x)) at x, so fderiv ℝ φ x v = q(L(v, Du(x) v)) for all v ∈ ℝⁿ.
6. (Injective derivative, parent step 6.) Let x ∈ Ω and suppose fderiv ℝ φ x v = fderiv ℝ φ x w. By step 5, q(L(v, Du(x) v)) = q(L(w, Du(x) w)); q is injective, so L(v, Du(x) v) = L(w, Du(x) w), and by step 2, v = w. Hence fderiv ℝ φ x is injective for every x ∈ Ω.
7. Steps 3, 4 and 6 are exactly the three conjuncts of the claim.
proof_key_steps: graphPoint a b = L(a, b) with L = finAddEquivProd.symm (sibling lemma), so φ = (q ∘ L)(·, u ·) + x₀
L is injective, so graph points determine the base point
φ(x) = φ(x') ⇒ L(x, u x) = L(x', u x') ⇒ x = x'
φ is C¹ on Ω as a continuous linear map composed with the C¹ map x ↦ (x, u x), plus a constant
For x ∈ Ω (open): chain rule gives Dφ(x)v = q(L(v, Du(x)v))
Dφ(x)v = Dφ(x)w ⇒ L(v, Du(x)v) = L(w, Du(x)w) ⇒ v = w
